title: The 9 Best Affirmation Apps, and Who Each One Is For
description: The 9 best affirmation apps in 2026, grouped by how you practise — guided, widgets, your own voice, audio, journaling, speaking aloud or one short card: MyBeing, I am, ThinkUp, Innertune, Mantra, Gratitude, Believe, Motivation and Anicca, checked against US App Store listings in November 2026.
markdown:
By Anicca · November 2026

Updated November 2026

There is no single best affirmation app, and any list that names one is dodging the real question. The right app depends on how you want to meet the words: read them on your Lock Screen, hear them in your own voice, say them out loud, or write them yourself.

**The short answer to "what are the best affirmation apps?":** there is no single winner. Among the apps we checked against their US App Store listings in November 2026, MyBeing walks you through a guided practice, I am has the biggest library and the most polish, ThinkUp leads on hearing the words in your own voice, Innertune on listening, Mantra on calm design, Gratitude on journaling, Believe on saying the words out loud, and Motivation on quotes rather than a practice. Anicca, our own app, is covered last and honestly: it does one narrow job, a short card of words chosen for the day you are actually having, and it does not do widgets, audio or voice recording.

This guide sorts the main apps by that choice. It also covers the two things these lists almost never mention, which are what the research says about how affirmations actually work and when they can misfire.

## What makes the best affirmation app for you

Start with delivery, not the feature list. An app you have to remember to open will fade by week two.

So how the words reach you matters more than how many there are.

Four things decide whether an app sticks. Do the words arrive on their own, can you change them, whose voice says them, and does the free tier let you practise at all?

Delivery is the one people underrate. A line on your Lock Screen gets seen on the days you least feel like opening anything.

Those are the days it counts.

Being able to change the words comes second. Someone else's line, written for a life you don't have, is easy to swipe past. Most apps let you write your own, though it's often buried in the settings.

The evidence under all this is about the practice, not any product. Cohen and Sherman's 2014 review found that short self-affirmation tasks improved how people did in health, school and relationships, sometimes months later.

What no study has done is compare one app with another. So treat every ranking, this one included, as a guide to fit rather than proof of quality.

## Who publishes these lists, and why it matters

Most of the pages that rank for this phrase are published by companies that make an affirmation app. In several of them, the winning app belongs to the people who wrote the page.

We're in the same boat. Anicca is ours, so read our bit with that in mind.

We won't pretend to be neutral. What we can do is tell you what each app is shaped for, and say plainly where ours is the wrong pick. Anicca appears last on this list, not first, for exactly that reason.

## The 9 best affirmation apps, grouped by how you practise

Prices and features below were checked in November 2026 against each app's US App Store listing. They change often and differ by country, so look at your own store page before paying for anything.

These are numbered for reading order, not merit. The other eight are here because each one beats ours for somebody.

We also checked when each app last shipped an update, which most lists on this subject don't bother with. An app can still be good months after its last release, but a long gap tells you something about whether anyone is still looking after it.

One of the nine is badly overdue, and we've said so in its entry.

### 1. MyBeing, for being walked through it rather than handed a list

Most apps on this page give you a card and leave the rest to you. MyBeing reads the day's affirmation aloud and builds a short breathing cycle around it, so the practice has a beginning and an end.

You can write your own lines too, and decide whether they mix in with the day's set, come first, or are the only ones you see. There are 81 topics, and a tone setting that changes the words between "I am" and "you are".

It's free to start on iPhone, with a paid tier for the rest. When we checked in November 2026 it stood at 4.7 stars from just 3 US ratings, version 1.0.7, last updated 20 November 2026.

Being straight about it: MyBeing is iPhone only for now, and it launched this year with a handful of ratings against I am's 740,210. If you're on Android, or a long track record is what you want, it isn't it yet.

### 2. I am, for the biggest library and the most polish

The most established app in the category, with 4.8 stars from 740,210 US ratings when we checked in November 2026, a very large library and widgets that work properly. If you want the safe, well-trodden choice, this is the one.

Two things to weigh before you install. Its App Store listing names advertising among the app's contents, and its paid tiers have run to $59.99 a year or $149.99 for life.

Last updated 18 November 2026 (version 7.10.0), so it's actively maintained. Worth knowing that Motivation, number 8 below, comes from the same developer, Monkey Taps, and shipped the same version number in the same week.

### 3. ThinkUp, for hearing the words in your own voice

ThinkUp has you record the affirmations yourself, then plays them back over music. Hearing your own voice say the line is a different experience from reading it, and for some people that's what makes it land.

The free tier is tight: a few recorded affirmations and one background track. That's still enough to find out whether the method suits you, which is all a free tier really has to do.

One caution, and it's the reason this app isn't higher. ThinkUp was last updated on 3 August 2025 (version 1.18.11, 4.7 stars from 7,522 US ratings), which is more than a year ago.

The app still runs and the method still stands. But a year without a release means no fixes when iOS changes under it, so think hard before buying the lifetime tier.

### 4. Innertune, for listening rather than reading

Built around audio, so it fits a walk, a commute, or the half hour before sleep. The paid tier advertises a very large library of affirmations, hundreds of playlists and a choice of voices.

Pick it if you'd rather not look at a screen. It's also the easiest one to let turn into background noise, which is the risk with anything you play while doing something else.

Last updated 5 November 2026 (version 6.14.3), and shipping regularly. It stood at 4.8 stars from 12,228 US ratings when we checked.

### 5. Mantra, for wanting the thing to feel calm

Simple cards, soft audio, careful typography. That sounds like decoration until you remember that an app which feels like a chore gets deleted in week two.

It's usually listed as iPhone only, so check before you plan a routine around it. The library is smaller than I am's, which is the trade for the quieter feel. It stood at 4.8 stars from 34,503 US ratings when we checked.

Actively maintained, and only just. Mantra sat quiet for months before an update on 19 October 2026 (version 5.9.7), so it's current again after a long quiet spell.

### 6. Gratitude, for people who already journal

Gratitude: Self-Care Journal puts affirmations beside journal entries, prompts and a vision board, so the line connects to something you actually wrote. If you already keep a journal, that's one app instead of two.

The trade is density. There's more to learn here than in a single-purpose app, and more to ignore once you've found the two features you want.

The most recently updated app on this page when we checked, at 22 November 2026 (version 6.0.4), and the best rated at 4.9 stars from 45,003 US ratings.

### 7. Believe, for saying them out loud

Built around speaking affirmations rather than reading them, including a mode where you say them while looking at your own face. People split hard on this one.

Give it a single day before you judge it. Either the directness works for you or it makes you want to put the phone down, and you'll know almost immediately.

Last updated 15 November 2026 (version 11.3.0). It's the smallest established app here by audience, with 379 US ratings at 4.9 stars, rather than tens of thousands.

### 8. Motivation, for a lift rather than a practice

Motivation serves quotes rather than first-person affirmations, which makes it a different thing in similar clothing. Someone else's words can pick you up, but they don't do what repeating your own line does.

Choose it if you want pleasant interruptions through the day. Skip it if you want a practice.

It has the largest audience of anything here, at 1,081,218 US ratings and 4.8 stars, and was last updated 18 November 2026 (version 7.10.0). Same developer as I am, which explains why the two feel so alike.

### 9. Anicca, for one short card chosen for the day you are having

This is our app, so weigh this entry accordingly.

Anicca does not give you a library to browse, a widget, audio, or a microphone. You answer questions about your life once, and the app puts a short card of words in front of you, chosen for that person and that day, and keeps changing them while you stay. It is built for the hard day, the rumination loop and the morning you do not feel like opening anything complicated.

The honest limits: it is iPhone only, it is small and new — version 1.11.0, last updated 22 November 2026, with a 5.0 rating from a single US rating when we checked, against I am's 740,210 — and if you want widgets, your own voice, or a journal, every app above does that job and we don't. The full picture is on the [Anicca product page](https://aniccaai.com/affirmation-app).

Anicca is free to download, with Anicca Premium at $59.99 a year after a 3-day free trial.

## What should an affirmation app cost?

Every major affirmation app is free to download and sells a paid plan. So the download price tells you nothing.

What varies is how much of the practice sits behind the wall.

The spread is wide. Yearly plans in this category ran from about $35 to about $60 when lists in this space checked in 2026, and some apps sell a one-off lifetime plan from roughly $80 to $150.

Lifetime deals deserve a pause. They look thrifty, and they only pay off if you still open the app in a year (on current habits, most people won't).

There's also the ad question, and the store page answers it before you install. Apple lists advertising under what an app contains, so you can check without downloading.

Our advice: pay nothing in week one. If an app can't hold you for a fortnight on its free tier, a yearly plan won't fix that.

## Does a big affirmation library matter?

Less than the marketing suggests. A library of 20,000 lines is the easiest thing to advertise and the hardest to show matters.

Think about how you actually use one. You want a handful of lines that fit your life this month, not a catalogue to browse.

There's a point where more gets worse. Scrolling a huge list is a decision every morning, and decisions are what kill daily habits.

Where size does help is range. If your life needs words about money, a new baby and a hard manager, a thin library runs out fast. That's a fair reason to prefer a bigger one.

## Should your affirmations say "I am" or "you are"?

This is the choice nobody asks about, and it may matter more than the app itself. Most apps give you first-person lines only.

Kross and colleagues found in 2014 that people who spoke to themselves as "you", or by name, handled stress better than people who used "I". The shift seems to put a little distance between you and your own feelings.

> I am steady, even now.

> You are steady, even now.

Read both and notice which one you believe. If one wording feels false and the other doesn't, that's useful information, whichever app you end up with.

## When an affirmation app is the wrong choice

Sometimes it is, and no list on this subject seems willing to say so. Wood's 2009 study found that people who already felt bad about themselves felt worse after repeating a kind line about themselves.

That should change how you shop. The warmest, most flattering app isn't automatically the kindest one for you.

A line far from what you believe can push you the wrong way.

The fix is usually smaller words, not no words. "I am learning to speak kindly to myself" lands easier than "I love myself completely".

> One honest limit: Anicca is not a medical or mental health service, and nor is any app on this page. If you are struggling with your mental health, please talk to a professional.

## How to test an affirmation app without wasting money

Download two, not six. Pick the two whose delivery style matches how you want to meet the words, and give each a fortnight.

Ask the free tier the hard question. Can you do the core practice without paying, or does it stop you after three days?

A trial is not a free tier. That difference is where most of the annoyance in this category lives.

Then wait longer than feels natural before judging. A 2025 review that pooled 129 tests from earlier studies, covering nearly 18,000 people, found the effects were often bigger after the practice ended than during it.

That's the trap in app shopping. You'll want a verdict in four days. The honest timeline is longer, which is why a free tier you can live in for a month beats a cheap annual plan bought on day one.

If you want the deeper comparisons behind this page, see our [flagship guide to the best affirmation apps](https://aniccaai.com/blog/best-affirmation-apps-2026-11-05), yesterday's [best daily affirmation apps](https://aniccaai.com/blog/best-daily-affirmation-apps-2026-11-22) comparison, and our [best sleep affirmation apps](https://aniccaai.com/blog/best-sleep-affirmation-apps-2026-11-21) roundup.

## Frequently asked questions

**What is the best affirmation app?**

There isn't one. The best affirmation app is the one that matches how you want to meet the words: guided practice (MyBeing), library and widgets (I am), your own voice (ThinkUp), listening (Innertune), calm cards (Mantra), journaling (Gratitude), speaking aloud (Believe), quotes (Motivation), or one short card chosen for your day (Anicca).

**What is the best free affirmation app?**

All of the main affirmation apps are free to download, so the real question is what the free tier gives you. Some let you use the core practice for free and charge for extra themes or voices. Others stop you after a few days, which is a trial rather than a free tier.

**Do affirmation apps actually work?**

The research is about the practice, not the apps. Cohen and Sherman's 2014 review found that short self-affirmation tasks improved outcomes in health, school and relationships, sometimes months later. No study has tested whether one app works better than another.

**Is the I am app free?**

I am is free to download. Its App Store listing names advertising among the app's contents, and its paid tiers have run to $59.99 a year and $149.99 for lifetime access in 2026 checks.

**Which affirmation app is best for Android?**

Fewer affirmation apps support Android well, and several of the best known ones are iPhone only. I am, ThinkUp and Gratitude all run on both, so start there if you are on Android. MyBeing and Anicca are iPhone only for now.

**How long should I use an affirmation app before deciding?**

Two weeks is a fair test. A 2025 review that pooled 129 earlier tests found that effects were often larger after the practice ended than during it, so a week is too short to judge.

**Which affirmation apps are still being updated?**

When we checked in November 2026, every app here except ThinkUp had shipped an update within the previous five weeks. ThinkUp was last updated in August 2025, more than a year earlier, which is worth a second thought before you buy its yearly or lifetime plan.
